messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: rstan wishlist
parts:
There are some things I don't think rstan does (using the development
version, but perhaps the help files don't reflect all recent work) that
I would like it to do.

1. extract() has options to include or exclude warmup. It would be nice
to have an option to specify the warmup period if, for example, I run
2,000 iterations (with the default half of them warmup) but decide that
things seemed to have converged after fewer than 1,000 iterations.

Or is it not a good idea to use the warmup period, during which it is
tuning parameters?

2. It would be nice if extract() could produce a 2 dimensional matrix,
with iterations (from all chains) as rows and parameters as columns.

3. It would be nice if monitor() could be called directly on a stanfit
object.

4. A convenient method to get effective sample size would be nice.

5. A convenient method to get an overall summary of how the model has
performed, perhaps the distribution of n_eff and rhat across parameters,
would be very useful in assessing performance. I and others have fallen
into the trap of assessing performance using time/iteration instead of
time/n_eff; I suspect part of the reason is that it is not easy to pull
out the n_effs and not obvious how one should summarize all the
different n_effs.

All of this can be obtained with suitable code; it would be helpful if
that code were already in the package.

Some of these issues are not so pressing if one has a limited number of
parameters so that inspecting the printed summary of the fit is
practical. But even the plot() method (which does provide a quick
color-coded way to scan for bad rhat) breaks down when there are too
many parameters.

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan wishlist
parts:
On 9/27/13 4:59 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> There are some things I don't think rstan does (using the development
> version, but perhaps the help files don't reflect all recent work) that
> I would like it to do.
>
> 1. extract() has options to include or exclude warmup. It would be nice
> to have an option to specify the warmup period if, for example, I run
> 2,000 iterations (with the default half of them warmup) but decide that
> things seemed to have converged after fewer than 1,000 iterations.

> Or is it not a good idea to use the warmup period, during which it is
> tuning parameters?

Not a good idea. The problem is that the warmup iterations
don't form a Markov chain, so none of our inferences from them
would be appropriate.

We've been considering some kind of auto-tuning that can turn
off adaptation on its own, but we haven't really figured out how
to monitor the statistics we need efficiently as samples come in
or figured out a good methodology for stopping.

> 2. It would be nice if extract() could produce a 2 dimensional matrix,
> with iterations (from all chains) as rows and parameters as columns.

The method on stanfit called as.mcmc.list is close, I think.
I'm so bad with R, I'm not even sure how to figure out what
the type of an object is.

> 3. It would be nice if monitor() could be called directly on a stanfit
> object.

I believe print() does that, but are you talking about
getting the return value? Is that why you want (2) above, to
provide input to monitor()? (I have to admit I haven't played with
many of these functions in RStan.)
> 4. A convenient method to get effective sample size would be nice.
Agreed. Should this be a method on stanfit?

> 5. A convenient method to get an overall summary of how the model has
> performed, perhaps the distribution of n_eff and rhat across parameters,
> would be very useful in assessing performance. I and others have fallen
> into the trap of assessing performance using time/iteration instead of
> time/n_eff; I suspect part of the reason is that it is not easy to pull
> out the n_effs and not obvious how one should summarize all the
> different n_effs.

The new command line bin/print does in fact print out n_eff/s for
each parameter. We should add that to RStan, too.

> All of this can be obtained with suitable code; it would be helpful if
> that code were already in the package.
Agreed.

> Some of these issues are not so pressing if one has a limited number of
> parameters so that inspecting the printed summary of the fit is
> practical. But even the plot() method (which does provide a quick
> color-coded way to scan for bad rhat) breaks down when there are too
> many parameters.

It sure does. As does print, because the output's too long.

Plot is also slow (I don't know if there's a way to
make it faster --- it just seems to me that R plotting is pretty
slow).

- Bob

> I've been running chains of 2,000 iterations, and as far as I can tell

It is indeed wasteful in some situations to use half for warmup.
Usually it's when you need a very large number of effective samples
but convergence is fast.

Be careful about concluding things about convergence by eye.
Stan continues to adapt during warmup and this can be helpful
for sampling speed. So it can look from the traceplots like
you've converged, but spending some more time in warmup can help
with the number of effective samples/second during sampling.

Stan 2 is less wasteful of iterations in warmup, so specifying
a shorter warmup time should work better. Stan 1.3 will throw
away the adaptation from some of the later adaptation stages if
the warmup isn't an even multiple of the adaptation windows.

messages.author: 54788cf3a8eb8916
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan wishlist

I use the following slightly awkward code to pull the *minimum* of the effective sample sizes from a stanfit object...

get_min_neff <- function(fit) {
  min({summary(fit)}$summary[, 'n_eff'])
}

Bob - feel free to modify / take as is / reject / etc...

Note this is the minimum across all constrained and unconstrained parameters and it is based on all chains... it'd be a bit more work to pull each individually... or the parameters individually...

I wanted to do marginal density plots across different datasets, so I wanted to try and make them approximately comparable, so I "optimized" for an n_eff of 500 +/- 10%...

Kind regards,
Sean
